verdict.headline: Weekend tanker attacks near Hormuz put oil back in focus ahead of inflation data
verdict.label: Sunday: S&P 500 closed Fri at 7,811.54 (+0.59%, week about +1.1%), 7 pts under its 7,818.93 record; Nasdaq 27,366.17; 10Y ~5.24% (Wed high 5.331%); Brent ~$104 Fri; two tankers on fire in the Gulf Sat; BTC ~$83,095 Sun (+0.4% in 24h); Dec hike odds ~70%.
verdict.horizon: four trading sessions, Monday October 12 through Friday October 16 (stocks trade Monday; the bond market is shut for Columbus Day)
verdict.rationale_short:
What happened: no stock, bond or oil market has traded since Friday, when the S&P 500 closed at 7,811.54, about 1.1% higher on the week and 7 points under its October 6 record, and the ten-year yield ended near 5.24% after touching 5.331% on Wednesday. On Saturday the Gulf shipping war stepped up. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a loaded supertanker exploded after hitting a mine while using a route they had not approved; the UAE National Guard separately rescued 22 crew from a burning tanker, and neither side has named the ship or confirmed it is the same incident. The US military said a jet disabled a cargo ship trying to run its blockade of Iran, the fourth since July. Bitcoin, the only market trading, was near $83,095 Sunday morning, up about 0.4% in 24 hours.

What it means: Friday's oil price, around $104 for Brent, already assumed a closed or contested strait, so the question for Sunday evening's oil futures open is whether these attacks change the supply picture or just confirm it. The evidence points both ways. Crude flows through Hormuz had recovered to about prewar levels by early October, according to Kpler data cited by CNBC, but that recovery depends on a US-protected route along Oman's coast, and that is the route the Guards say they are now targeting. Eleven tankers were attacked in the week to October 4, the most since the war began, and Brent still finished below its highs, so markets have absorbed attacks before. What is uncertain: the IRGC's mine claim is unverified, and the tanker's identity, cargo and damage are not known.

What would change the picture: a clear jump in Brent when futures reopen at 6pm ET Sunday would feed straight into the inflation worry already in bond yields, days before September CPI on Wednesday, October 14. The Cleveland Fed's nowcast has headline inflation at about 3.6% for the year from 3.4%, with core forecasts clustered near 2.4%; a core monthly gain of 0.3% or more would likely push the ten-year back toward 5.331% and firm the roughly 70% futures-market odds of a December hike. JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo report Tuesday. An S&P 500 close above 7,818.93 would be a new record; a close under 7,666.45 would show weakness spreading. Conviction is low: it is a weekend, news pages could not be opened from this run so figures rest on search summaries of the cited sources, Friday's Brent settlement differs slightly across sources, and VIX and dollar-index closes were unavailable.
verdict.lede_short: Two tankers burned in the Gulf on Saturday and the US disabled a ship running its Iran blockade, so oil's reopening Sunday evening is the first test of the week. Crude flows had recovered to prewar levels on a US-protected route, which is the route Iran now says it is hitting. A jump in oil would add to inflation worry before Wednesday's CPI, with the S&P 500 7 points under its record and the ten-year near 5.24%.

supporting_data.label: The UAE National Guard rescued 22 crew from a burning oil tanker on Saturday while Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a loaded supertanker exploded after hitting a mine — neither has named the ship, so the mine claim is unverified, but it is the first reported mine strike on the route tankers have been using.

Crude moving through Hormuz reached a seven-day average of 13.5 million barrels a day in early October, about the prewar level, on a US-protected route along Oman's coast — the weekend attacks matter because they target the route that recovery depends on.

Eleven tankers were attacked crossing Hormuz in the week to October 4, the most since the war began, yet Brent ended last week near $104 — markets have absorbed a high pace of attacks before, so Sunday's oil reopening shows whether this weekend is treated as more of the same or a change.

US Central Command said a jet disabled a Panama-flagged cargo ship trying to run its blockade of Iran on Saturday, the fourth ship disabled and with 135 turned back since July 14 — the US is enforcing the blockade more forcefully even as President Trump calls talks with Iran productive.

The Cleveland Fed's nowcast puts September headline inflation at about 3.6% for the year, up from 3.4%, with core forecasts near 2.4% — energy drives the rise, so the core monthly figure on Wednesday is what decides whether rate-hike worry grows.

The S&P 500 closed Friday at 7,811.54, up about 1.1% on the week and 7 points under its October 6 record — stocks go into bank results and CPI near their peak, with little cushion if either disappoints.

The ten-year yield ended the week near 5.24% after touching 5.331% on Wednesday, its highest since 2002 — the bond market is shut Monday, so Tuesday is the first day yields can react to the weekend's Gulf news.
Bitcoin was near $83,095 on Sunday morning, up about 0.4% in 24 hours in an $82,707-83,194 range — the one market open through the Gulf news stayed calm and above Thursday's $80,320 low.

watchlist_mentions.note: Reports Tuesday, October 13, with Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo; loan losses and consumer spending are the figures that matter with the ten-year near 5.24% and oil near $104.
Oil producers are the first stocks to show how Monday's market reads the weekend tanker attacks, after Brent ended Friday near $104.

trade_setups.thesis: Saturday brought a claimed mine strike, a second tanker fire and a US strike on a blockade runner, on the southern route that had brought Hormuz crude flows back to about prewar levels. Friday's price near $104 already assumed a contested strait, so the open shows whether the attacks change the supply picture.
trade_setups.entry: Brent near $104 at Friday's close; futures reopen 6pm ET Sunday.
trade_setups.invalidation: A sustained jump on the reopen would say markets see the southern route at risk; a flat open would say the attacks are being read as part of the existing pattern.

trade_setups.thesis: The ten-year sits 9 basis points under Wednesday's 2002-era high, and futures price about a 70% chance of a December hike. Headline CPI is expected to rise on energy; core is forecast near 2.4% for the year.
trade_setups.entry: Ten-year ~5.24%; Wednesday's high 5.331%; Cleveland Fed nowcast about 3.6% headline.
trade_setups.invalidation: A core monthly gain of 0.3% or more would likely take the ten-year back toward 5.331%; 0.2% or less would ease hike pressure.

trade_setups.thesis: The index ended the week 7 points under its record after absorbing three separate shocks. Monday is the first session to price the weekend's Gulf news, ahead of bank results and CPI.
trade_setups.invalidation: A close above 7,818.93 would be a new record; a close under 7,666.45 would show weakness spreading beyond single sectors.
